title: Feedback sources in essay writing: peer-generated or AI-generated feedback?
venue: International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education
extended_summary:
This paper examines whether generative AI, specifically ChatGPT, can serve as a useful feedback source for essay writing and how its feedback quality compares with peer-generated feedback. The authors focus on argumentative essay writing, a complex task in which students often need substantial feedback but instructors may face workload constraints. The study asks two main questions: whether the quality of peer and ChatGPT feedback differs, and whether the quality of students’ essays is related to the quality of feedback produced by either source.

The intervention involved an online argumentative essay writing module delivered through Brightspace. In week one, students wrote individual essays on controversial food-science topics. In week two, students provided asynchronous peer feedback on classmates’ essays using FeedbackFruits, while the researchers also submitted the same essays to ChatGPT with a parallel prompt to generate AI feedback. The researchers then coded essay quality and feedback quality using established coding schemes and analyzed differences between peer and ChatGPT feedback with multivariate analysis, along with correlations between essay quality and feedback quality.

Participants were 74 graduate students in food sciences at a Dutch university during the 2022–2023 academic year. The context was higher education, not secondary school. The activity took place in an online learning environment over two weeks. Outcomes were based on coded analyses of essays and feedback rather than self-report.

The study found significant differences between peer and ChatGPT feedback. ChatGPT produced stronger descriptive feedback, often summarizing or describing essay content, whereas peers were better at identifying specific problems in essays. Overall, the authors argue that ChatGPT and peer feedback may play complementary roles rather than one fully replacing the other. They also found no overall significant relationship between essay quality and the overall quality of feedback generated by peers or ChatGPT. The paper concludes that ChatGPT shows promise as a feedback source in higher education writing tasks, but its use should be interpreted cautiously given the limited sample, single-site context, short duration, and absence of analysis of how students used the feedback for revision.
quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed empirical comparator study with systematic coding and statistical analysis, but it is exploratory, non-randomized, conducted in a single higher-education course, and not in the target K-12 population. It therefore fits correlational/comparison evidence with limited causal credibility rather than strong experimental evidence.
impact_tier_rationale: The study shows small, mixed differences between ChatGPT and peer feedback quality dimensions (η2=0.02-0.03) and does not measure downstream improvement in students’ writing performance. Impact on learning is therefore modest or unclear rather than clearly positive.

interventions.use_case: ChatGPT-generated automated feedback on graduate students’ argumentative essays, compared directly against peer-generated feedback using the same feedback prompt and coded for affective, cognitive, and constructive feedback quality.
ChatGPT was used as a generative AI conversational system to read students’ essays and produce feedback in natural language, functioning as an AI feedback source rather than a full tutor.

finding.finding_summary: In a direct comparison on essay-feedback quality for argumentative writing, ChatGPT and peer feedback differed significantly across specific feedback dimensions for 74 graduate students. ChatGPT produced stronger descriptive feedback (M=2.00, SD=0.00 vs peer M=1.91, SD=0.29; F(1,146)=3.25, p<0.05, η2=0.03), while peers were better at identifying problems in essays (M=1.52, SD=0.49 vs ChatGPT M=1.29, SD=0.70; F(1,146)=4.38, p<0.01, η2=0.02); no significant differences were found for affective, justification, or constructive components. The study did not test revision outcomes or improved final writing quality, only the quality of feedback on writing.
finding.measure: Coded quality of feedback on argumentative essays: affective, cognitive (description, identification, justification), and constructive components
finding.effect_size: η2=0.03 for description; η2=0.02 for identification
finding.std_deviation: Peer description SD=0.29; ChatGPT description SD=0.00; Peer identification SD=0.49; ChatGPT identification SD=0.70

finding.finding_summary: When framed as an LLM-based feedback source for essay writing, ChatGPT showed a different profile from peers rather than a uniformly superior or inferior one. It was more descriptive but less effective at pinpointing problems, and there was no evidence in this study that ChatGPT feedback improved students’ revised writing quality because revision effects were not measured.
finding.measure: Coded feedback-quality rubric applied to ChatGPT-generated essay feedback
finding.effect_size: η2=0.03 for higher description; η2=0.02 for lower identification relative to peers
finding.std_deviation: ChatGPT description SD=0.00; ChatGPT identification SD=0.70

finding.finding_summary: The study found no overall significant relationship between students’ essay quality and the quality of feedback generated by either peers or ChatGPT, suggesting that stronger writing performance did not generally translate into better feedback production. Some isolated correlations appeared for subcomponents (e.g., ChatGPT affective feedback with overall essay quality r=0.28, p<0.05; peer affective feedback with overall essay quality r=-0.23, p<0.05), but the overall pattern was null.
finding.measure: Spearman correlations between coded essay-quality components and coded feedback-quality components
finding.effect_size: r=0.28; r=-0.23 for selected subcomponents; overall relationship not significant
